intro: The Appassionata begins almost inaudibly, with both hands tracing a bare F-minor chord. Artur Schnabel plays a movement in which the gentlest tune can turn savage within a few bars.

sections.label: A · Bare octaves in F minor
sections.mNote: A broken chord, then three short notes and a long one

sections.label: B · The dolce tune in A♭
sections.mNote: A♭ major soon darkens to A♭ minor

sections.label: Dev · The opening in E major
sections.mNote: The quiet broken chord begins again in a distant key

sections.label: A′ · The opening above a C bass
sections.mNote: Repeated bass notes persist beneath the returning tune

sections.label: B′ · The dolce tune in F
sections.mNote: The melody returns in F major, then turns to minor

sections.label: Coda · D♭ and another storm
sections.mNote: The second tune returns in D♭ before the long slowing

sections.label: Coda · Faster, then quiet
sections.mNote: Più allegro in F minor, ending pianissimo

cues.title: A bare broken chord
cues.text: The hands move together in octaves, quietly tracing F minor. Then the same phrase shifts up a semitone. A small repeated-note figure answers it: three short notes and a long one, knocking from low on the keyboard.
cues.evidence: First edition, Bureau des Arts et d’Industrie, plate 521, p. 2, bars 1–17. Harmonic account: https://tonic-chord.com/beethoven-piano-sonata-no-23-in-f-minor-analysis/ . Facsimile: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A publisher names the sonata
cues.text: Hamburg, 1838: Cranz publishes a four-hand arrangement as Sonata appassionata. Beethoven has been dead for eleven years. The title sticks, although he never writes appassionato anywhere in the sonata.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus work catalogue, nickname and publication history: https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/5292968940404736 . Beethoven died in 1827.

cues.title: The gentle tune darkens
cues.text: A new melody rises through A♭ major, marked dolce — sweetly. It shares the opening’s broken-chord shape, now with an accompaniment. Within the same passage A♭ minor takes over, and the hands drive towards a much fiercer ending.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 3–4, bars 36–62: dolce second subject in A♭ major and its continuation in A♭ minor.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E major after A♭ minor
cues.text: The exposition sinks into A♭ minor. The bare opening phrase starts again in E major, a startlingly distant place. Beethoven carries it through new keys, then works on fragments of the gentler tune.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 4–7, development from bar 66. Tonic Chord identifies the E-major restatement and the use of both principal themes: https://tonic-chord.com/beethoven-piano-sonata-no-23-in-f-minor-analysis/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass will not leave
cues.text: The opening returns in F minor, but a repeated C keeps sounding beneath it. The first phrase once stood alone. Now the bass follows it like a second thought that will not be silenced.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 8, bars 136–140: return of the first subject over a dominant pedal on C. The pedal subsequently moves to D♭ and back to C.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schnabel leaves Berlin
cues.text: This is Schnabel’s 1933 recording. That year, with the Nazis in power, he leaves Germany with his family and settles in Italy. He has made Berlin his home for more than thirty years.
cues.evidence: Schnabel Music Foundation biography: Berlin from 1899, departure with his family in 1933, first to Italy. https://schnabelmusicfoundation.org/musicians/artur-schnabel/

cues.title: F major, briefly
cues.text: The dolce melody comes home in F major. For a while the sonata seems able to end in sunlight. Then F minor returns, repeating the major-to-minor change that overtook the tune in the exposition.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 9–10, bars 175–201: second subject in F major, followed by its F-minor continuation from bar 191.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another turn through D♭
cues.text: The coda brings back the opening’s broken chord and takes the second tune into D♭ major. Long runs cross the keyboard. Eventually Beethoven slows them with ritardando, then Adagio, holding the pianist at a fermata before the final rush.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 10–12: extended coda, second subject in D♭ at bar 211, then ritardando, Adagio and fermata before Più allegro.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A storm that whispers out
cues.text: Più allegro: faster. The second tune returns in F minor above the left hand’s repeated chords. The final rush spends itself, and the music sinks into a quiet F-minor ending.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 12–13: Più allegro, second-subject material in F minor at bar 241 and final six bars of tonic harmony.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The broken chord begins to sing
transitions.from: A · Bare octaves in F minor
transitions.to: B · The dolce tune in A♭
transitions.how: The fast triplet figures settle on E♭, the dominant of A♭ major, and diminish. The right hand begins a connected melody, marked dolce, above a separate accompaniment. Its rising broken chord recalls the shape of the opening.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 3, bars 25–40. Harmonic account: https://tonic-chord.com/beethoven-piano-sonata-no-23-in-f-minor-analysis/

transitions.title: The opening finds E major
transitions.from: B · The dolce tune in A♭
transitions.to: Dev · The opening in E major
transitions.how: The exposition closes quietly in A♭ minor. A short link leads to the opening broken chord in E major, with the hands once again exposed in octaves. There is no exposition repeat: this familiar phrase starts the development.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 4–5, bars 62–70: A♭-minor close and E-major opening of the development.

transitions.title: C stays beneath the returning tune
transitions.from: Dev · The opening in E major
transitions.to: A′ · The opening above a C bass
transitions.how: The development lingers on the dominant of F minor, with diminished harmony and the repeated-note figure pressing against C. The opening phrase returns, but the C pedal carries on underneath. The pianist must fit the familiar octaves around that persistent bass.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 7–8, bars 124–140: dominant preparation and return above the C pedal.

transitions.title: The sweet tune comes home
transitions.from: A′ · The opening above a C bass
transitions.to: B′ · The dolce tune in F
transitions.how: The bridge now prepares C, the dominant of F. Its quick figures subside, leaving the dolce melody in F major over a gently moving accompaniment. The major third will soon flatten as the continuation turns to F minor.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 8–10, bars 152–201: rewritten bridge, F-major second subject and F-minor continuation.

transitions.title: The quiet bass starts again
transitions.from: B′ · The dolce tune in F
transitions.how: The F-minor closing figures diminish, but their running notes continue into the coda. The opening broken chord returns low on the keyboard; the second tune then appears in D♭ major. Beethoven begins another stretch of developing these two phrases.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 10–11, coda from bar 201, extended at bar 205; second subject in D♭ major at bar 211.

transitions.title: A held C releases the rush
transitions.how: The runs break into short chords as Beethoven writes ritardando, then Adagio. A fermata holds the dominant harmony over C. Più allegro begins with forceful chords and sends the second tune back into F minor above the left hand’s repeated accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 12: ritardando, Adagio, fermata and Più allegro. Facsimile: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0

fields.note: The solo-piano work is identified, but Schnabel’s performing edition and any editorial alterations are not. No cut or take-splice history is supplied for this MP3.

fields.label: Label

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Bloesch identifies the original complete-sonata issue as HMV DB 2215–2217 in Beethoven Sonata Society Volume 5, part of set DB 2211–2217. The transferred pressing or reissue catalogue number is unknown. The embedded portrait contains no readable carrier identification.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Original session documentation assigns movement I to two sides, 2B 6605 and 2B 6606, with takes 2 listed as the issued masters; the catalogue lists 2B 6605II and 2B 6606II. fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is credited for this file. The Archive uploader recordplayer78 is not equated with an engineer or owner. Andrew Rose’s credit on the separately consulted Pristine reissue is not transferred to this MP3; no upstream link to that reissue is established.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive added/public date is 27 March 2020. The embedded date tag is 2001, without an identified release or transfer to which it refers. Neither date establishes when the analogue source was transferred or restored.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: The MP3’s encoder tag states ‘Audiograbber 1.83.01, LAME dll 3.99, 256 Kbit/s, Joint Stereo, Normal quality’.
fields.note: Inspection of the downloaded selected stream found MP3 audio at 44,100 Hz, two channels and 256,000 bit/s, plus an attached JPEG portrait. Two-channel encoding is not evidence of an original stereo session. Analogue transfer equipment, equalisation, noise reduction, pitch/speed correction, restoration and edit history remain unknown. Archive calls the file ‘VBR MP3’; that repository format label is distinct from the inspected stream and encoder tag.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: The underlying Beethoven composition is public domain under the ordinary EU life-plus-70 term.
fields.note: Beethoven died in 1827. The cited original score contains the historical composition; no unidentified modern performing edition is cleared by this term calculation. Composition rights are separate from the rights in Schnabel’s recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934.
fields.note: The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly gives 1934 as the first release of HMV DB 2211–2217; Bloesch identifies Op. 57 within that issue as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610. Publication is thus documented separately from the 11 April 1933 session. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established and no worldwide clearance is claimed. The Archive’s Public Domain Mark is an assertion, not an ownership release; the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not relied upon. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
